title: How to split the pot when the game stops early
description:
First to 3 rounds wins 64 coins, and the game stops at 2 to 1. Splitting by the score (2 to 1, about 43 and 21) was the textbook answer from Pacioli in 1494. Pascal's answer, in his letter to Fermat of 29 July 1654: count the rounds each player still needs, and imagine one more round. Win it and you take all 64; lose it and it's 2 to 2, an even split of 32 each. So 32 is yours either way and half of the other 32: 48 to 16, 3 to 1. Fermat got the same by playing out all 4 possible endings: you win 3. Their letters on this problem are where probability theory starts.

Numbers checked in code: exact fractions with Pascal's and Fermat's methods, plus 200,000 simulated finishes of the game (you win 75.05%). Sources: Wikipedia, Problem of points; Pascal's letter of 29 July 1654 (IREM Caen, 'Les partis chez Pascal et Fermat').

Pacioli (Summa, 1494) split by rounds won; the Chevalier de Méré posed the problem to Pascal around 1654, solved in the Pascal-Fermat correspondence; Fermat's method plays out r+s-1 more rounds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problem_of_points)

Pascal's letter of 29 July 1654: 32 pistoles each (64), first to 3; one player needs 1, the other 2: win -> 64, lose -> 2-2, 32 each; so 48 and 16 (https://irem-archive.unicaen.fr/IMG/pdf/les_partis_chez_pascal_et_fermat.pdf, https://gtfp.cs.rhul.ac.uk/pulskamp/Pascal/Sources/pasfer.pdf)

beats.say: You stop at 2 to 1. Split 2 to 1, or 3 to 1?
Splitting by the score sounds fair. It was the textbook answer for 160 years. It's wrong.
Paris, 1654. A nobleman asks Blaise Pascal: first to 3 wins 64 coins, but the game stops at 2 to 1.
Don't count the rounds you won. Count the rounds you still need. You need 1. They need 2.
Play one more round in your head. Win it, and you take all 64.
Lose it: 2 to 2, a coin flip. 32 each.
So 32 is yours either way. Only the other 32 is in doubt.
Half of it is yours: 48 to 16. 3 to 1, not 2 to 1.
Fermat checked it another way: 4 possible endings, you win 3. Those letters started probability.
Same game, but you lead 1 to 0. What's your share of the 64?
